title: Pleased with Allah as Lord
hookLine: I am pleased with Allah as Lord, Islam as religion, Muhammad ﷺ as prophet (Abu Dawud)
tomorrow: what do sins and sea foam have in common?

cards: 'Fine' can close a conversation. 'Content' opens one. Somewhere past both is an Arabic word, radiitu: I'm pleased, I'm satisfied, I accept it gladly.

It's the heart of a line taught for the morning and evening, and it answers yesterday's question about saying it out loud: I am pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad ﷺ as prophet.

teach.b: In Abu Dawud, whoever says it in the morning and the evening is promised that God will please him on the Day of Resurrection. Pleased, and pleased in return.
Sahih Muslim has a sweeter version of the same idea: whoever is pleased with Allah as Lord, Islam as religion and Muhammad as messenger has tasted the sweetness of faith.
Tasted, like something on the tongue; that's the detail to tell someone tonight.
Being pleased isn't pretending every day is good. It's naming what you're glad to belong to, on good days and hard ones.
Now the week, all of it. A man wrapped in his cloak, told to rise in the night: stand, recite. Givers who wanted no thanks: for his sake.
The short surahs at the back of the book: the first part you knew. A pace for a lifetime: the book, for life. A line that names the favor and the fault: you are my lord.
Words for the two edges of the day, edges a neighbor tradition keeps too: nothing harms with his name.
Six lines, and one word to hold them together: pleased.

how: Muslims who keep the morning and evening remembrances may include this line, said three times; a version of it is also said after hearing the call to prayer.

games.q: what does “pleased with allah as lord” mean?
o: saying sorry for complaining about a hard day
saying gladly that you accept God, faith and prophet
saying you put up with whatever life hands you

games.q: the week, matched — tap the pairs.

s: being pleased with God means pretending every day is good
it's naming what you're glad to belong to, on good days and hard ones.
Sahih Muslim calls it tasting the sweetness of faith
whoever is pleased with Allah as Lord, Islam as religion and Muhammad as messenger has tasted it.
this week's protection line comes straight from the Qur'an
it comes from the Prophet's sayings, in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi.

games.q: a friend's summer plans fell through, and she says 'i'm fine' through her teeth. which reply is closest to radiitu?
o: 'it's okay to hurt. what are you still glad to belong to?'
'don't worry, everything happens for a reason you'll see soon.'
games.why: the line isn't swallowing the hurt. it's naming what you're glad of, with the hurt still there.

practice: Count three things on your fingers that you're glad of right now. Not the big ones; the close ones: a voice you heard today, something you ate, the chair under you. For each, say quietly: pleased.
If you pray, end with the line itself, once.

wordCard.voice: Pleased with Allah as Lord: a line for morning and evening, with radiitu, I'm pleased, at its center.

orig.note: Arabic: I am pleased, I am content; the line's first word.

carryVoice: Keep this: pleased, not fine, not resigned, but glad of it. A week, gathered up.

sources.ref: Sunan Abu Dawud 5072 (pleased with Allah as Lord, morning and evening)
